title: Battleships in the dark off Guadalcanal

facts.text: In mid November 1942, Japan made one more big push to retake Guadalcanal: a convoy of troop transports, covered by warships sent to shell Henderson Field, the American airfield on the island.
In the first night action, on 13 November, an American cruiser force threw itself into the Japanese battleships at close range. Rear Admirals Daniel Callaghan and Norman Scott were both killed.
On 14 November, American planes caught the Japanese transports by day and sank six, with a seventh later lost.
That night Rear Adm. Willis Lee brought the battleships Washington and South Dakota and four destroyers into the waters off Savo Island to meet a Japanese force led by the battleship Kirishima.
All four American destroyers were knocked out early. Preston, Walke, and Benham were lost.
South Dakota suffered an electrical failure that knocked out her power and radar, and was then lit up and hit 26 or 27 times before she pulled away.

Washington, tracking the enemy by radar in the dark, closed to about 8,400 yards and hit Kirishima with about nine 16 inch shells and many smaller ones. The Japanese fired torpedoes at her and missed.
Kirishima capsized and sank at 03:25 on 15 November 1942.

Four Japanese transports beached themselves at Tassafaronga and were destroyed by planes and artillery the next morning. Only 2,000 to 3,000 of the troops got ashore, and most of their food and ammunition was lost.
In the night action of 14 to 15 November, 242 Americans and 249 Japanese sailors died.
It was Japan's last major attempt to take back control of the seas around Guadalcanal or retake the island.

photoNote: USS Washington fires her main battery during the night action off Guadalcanal, 14 November 1942. U.S. Navy photo, public domain (via Wikimedia Commons, 1920 px). Dark night photo with muzzle flash; the most dramatic still for the Story Card opening (Test C).

photo.caption: Two of the beached Japanese transports burn on the Guadalcanal shore the morning after the battle.

declassified.fact: This was one of only two fights in the whole Pacific war in which battleships fought each other on the surface. The other came two years later at Surigao Strait during the Battle of Leyte Gulf.

film.shot_notes: No usable public domain film of the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal was found. The famous Navy footage of Japanese torpedo planes attacking U.S. transports off Guadalcanal on 12 November 1942 could not be located on the NARA catalog (428-NPC-16882 is Paramount News; 428-NPC-16103 shows the August 1942 air attacks). The night actions were not filmed.
